item.title: It Matters Why You Move In Together
item.description:
Relationships

It Matters Why You Move In Together

Cohabitation reasons predict relationship quality and future.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Cohabitation is common in the U.S., both for couples who intend to marry and those who don't.
  • The reasons for cohabiting may be an important indicator of relationship quality.
  • Research suggests that intrinsic reasons predict higher relationship quality than extrinsic reasons.
  • Reasons for cohabiting do not appear to affect the trajectory of relationships.

Cohabitation (prior to or instead of marriage) is common and normative among young couples in the U.S., yet the reasons people decide to move in together are varied. Many believe that living together before marriage is patently beneficial, a kind of "test drive before buying" approach. Some past research, however, has suggested that premarital cohabitation can be associated with poorer marital outcomes. In some studies, long-term cohabiting couples with no plans to get marries report higher frequency of conflict, physical aggression, and risk for separation than those who enter directly into marriage or cohabit as a stepping stone to marriage.

To be sure, cohabiting is not a one-size-fits-all proposition. Some long-term cohabiting couples experience decreasing relationship quality, declines in relationship satisfaction and dedication, and increases in negative communication, but recent research finds that many others have satisfying relationships, particularly those who enter cohabitation with an intent to marry (Interestingly, one study found that those in Living-Apart-Together [LAT] relationships with no intentions to live together had the lowest levels of relationship satisfaction).

Why Does Cohabitation Work for Some Couples But Not Others?

Psychologists are interested in those aspects of cohabiting that may predict relationship quality and future prospects. One potential such factor is people’s reasons for moving in together. Broadly, research has shown that those who move in for intrinsic reasons (wanting to spend more time together) tend to report better outcomes than those who move in for extrinsic reasons (financial savings). Existing work on this topic, however, has largely been cross-sectional, thus precluding an examination of relationship functioning over time.

Source: flutie 8211 for Pixabay

An interesting question yet to be answered is whether differences in relationship quality linked to reasons for cohabitation predate couples’ decision to cohabitate. Longitudinal studies may provide clarity about whether couples’ reasons for joining forces either reflect existing relationship quality (selection effect) or impact relationship trajectories into the future (experience effect).

A recent study by Claire Chapman and colleagues at the University of Denver (2026) sought to close this knowledge gap. The authors focused on how three common reasons for cohabitation—to spend more time together, to test the relationship, and convenience—predicted relationship outcomes (staying together or breaking up) and satisfaction over a five-year period. Participants were 485 adults (68 percent female) in romantic, heterosexual relations who were either already cohabiting or entered cohabitation during the study.

Data were collected about participants’ reasons for the decision and their relationship status and functioning using multiple waves of surveys. Participants reported their reasons for entering cohabitation, and periodically completed measures of relationship quality including satisfaction, negative communication, and dedication.

The results were intriguing. By the end of the study, 139 (28.7 percent) experienced relationship dissolution. Stronger endorsement of "testing the relationship" as a reason for cohabitation predicted a higher likelihood of breakup, while spending time together or convenience reasons did not predict relationship breakup, even after controlling for demographic (including gender, age, race, education, employment status, and individual annual income) and relationship variables (i.e., relationship status and relationship duration).

Regarding relationship functioning, stronger endorsement of "spending more time together" as a reason for cohabiting was significantly associated with higher relationship satisfaction, lower negative communication, and higher dedication post-cohabitation, while endorsement of "testing the relationship" was significantly associated with lower relationship satisfaction, higher negative communication, and lower dedication following cohabitation. Interestingly, the reason of "convenience" was not associated with any aspect of relationship functioning.

Additionally, results showed that time (since entering cohabitation) significantly affected relationship satisfaction. Specifically, relationship satisfaction declined over time and negative communication increased regardless while dedication remained constant over time regardless of reasons for cohabitation.

In other words, reasons for cohabiting did not interact with the passage of time to predict any of the three indicators of relationship functioning. This suggests that reasons for cohabitation did not affect overtime relationship trajectories following cohabitation. The authors note: “people who endorsed varying levels of each reason followed similar trajectories of relationship functioning after cohabitation (albeit, at different levels)… Reasons for cohabitation appeared to reflect couples’ relationship quality at the time of moving in together rather than altering its trajectories.”

Overall, couples who cohabited to test their relationship entered cohabitation with lower preexisting relationship quality, compared to the other two reasons. Testing the relationship, (but not spending time together or convenience), predicted odds of breakup after moving in together.

It appears that people who decide to enter cohabitation to test the relationship may already be experiencing doubts and may hope that the act of moving in together will strengthen the relationship, yet these hopes may be more likely to collapse under the weight of living together. In this way, moving in to test the relationship may, perhaps ironically, indeed provide a useful test.

Future research may inquire about cohabiting couples' predictions regarding their relationship success down the road. Do those who move in to "test the relationship" predict they will succeed, or fail? We'll await the science.

item.title: What Do I Do When I Cannot Walk Outside?
item.description:
Aging

What Do I Do When I Cannot Walk Outside?

Loneliness and social isolation in a time of climate crisis.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Walking is the number one health promoting physical activity for older adults.
  • Increased physical activity, such as walking, boosts positive emotions and personal and social resilience.
  • With increasing heat, as temperatures exceed 90°F for days, walking becomes dangerous, even deadly.
  • Walking helps combat loneliness and social isolation.
The Benefits of Nature Walking
Source: Jasmin Tahmaseb McConatha

It is early July 2026; temperatures are above 90°F (32 degrees Celsius) for several consecutive days. Dina, who is 102 years old, has been unable to take her daily walk in the park near her home because of the extreme heat. After several days indoors, she begins to feel sluggish and lonely. Weather permitting, most mornings Dina drives the short distance to a large park near her home, where she walks a one-mile loop. During her walks, she regularly stops to chat with acquaintances she has come to know over the years, several of whom she also occasionally sees socially. These daily interactions are an important and enjoyable part of her day.

Dina has loving family and friends who she sees when their schedules permit. But her walk is at her discretion and under her control, weather permitting. Walking keeps her fit, provides her with regular social connection, and maintains a connection to her community. For Dina, the park is far more than a place to exercise, it is one of her lifelines. Her daily walk also helps protect her from loneliness and social isolation. At the same time, it reinforces a sense of control, optimism, and independence that have characterized her long life.

Staying Active at 102
Source: With Permission by Jasmin Tahmaseb McConatha

As periods of extreme heat become more frequent and prolonged, Dina is increasingly confined to her home. At her age, walking outdoors in temperatures above 90°F poses significant health risks, leaving her with few safe alternatives. Although she has always been energetic and optimistic, the loss of her daily walks and the resulting isolation are beginning to affect her mood and well-being.

Dina’s experience is not unique. Although at 102 she is amazing, studies inform us that older adults of all ages walk for well-being and social connection. In fact, walking is the most popular form of physical activity in later life. As Dina’s case illustrates, climate-related heat can undermine not only physical activity, but also social connections made during walking. According to AARP (2022) more than 80% of older adults walk regularly, and even among adults aged 85 years and older, like Dina, more than 40% walk as their primary form of exercise. Walking is also inexpensive and accessible if safe walking spaces are available, which unfortunately is not always the case (Tahmaseb McConatha, et al., 2023). Green spaces are not equally distributed; poor older adults often lack a safe place to walk. For those who can, walking is a practical way for older adults to remain physically and socially active. For only 30 minutes, 5 times a week, physical and mental health can be improved. Research has long established that in addition to physical health benefits, walking promotes psychological well-being, social connection and engagement, as well as community participation. Even ten minutes of walking can improve mood, reduce stress, and enhance well-being.

In my ongoing work examining factors that promote well-being and protect against loneliness and social isolation in later life, walking has consistently emerged as one of the most effective and health-promoting activities. In addition to improving cardiovascular health, strength, and mobility, walking increases opportunities for social interaction, strengthens community connections, improves mood, and reduces the risk of anxiety and depression. Group walks, neighborhood strolls, and walks through parks and community spaces provide opportunities for natural, interpersonal, and social connections, making walking an important strategy for addressing loneliness and social isolation in later life.

The benefits of walking are even more crucial as loneliness and social isolation have emerged as a global public health crisis. The World Health Organization's Commission on Social Connection (2025) reported that approximately one in six people worldwide experience loneliness, a condition that also contributes to an estimated 871,000 premature deaths annually. Loneliness and social isolation affect individuals across the life course, with younger adults being the loneliest, but older adults are particularly vulnerable given later life challenges that include role loss, such as retirement, loss of friends and family, chronic illness, mobility limitations, and living alone.

As social networks shrink, walking, temperature permitting, becomes increasingly important for well-being. Walking can increase social connections and boost positive emotions. Fredrickson’s (2001) broaden-and-build theory states that participation in meaningful and fulfilling activities such as walking increases positive emotions while helping individuals manage negative ones. The theory is useful in illustrating the ways that positive emotions can emerge from increased physical and social activity and as a result increase individual and social resilience. In my work, I have found that walking is a personally rewarding activity, in addition to the above-mentioned benefits, it also promotes a sense of control, and enhances meaning, purpose, and life satisfaction.

The benefits of Natural Connection
Source: Jasmin Tahmaseb McConatha

Walking in green spaces is particularly beneficial. Green spaces have the potential to provide a comforting environment, further fostering well-being. The many health benefits of connecting with natural spaces, forest bathing, and immersing oneself in nature are receiving considerable attention. Walking in parks and natural environments provides additional benefits for renewal, stress reduction, improving mood, and strengthening feelings of connectedness to nature.

Currently one of the greatest emerging threats to these benefits is climate change. As global temperatures continue to rise, extreme heat is becoming more common. On days when temperatures exceed 90°F, instead of promoting well-being, outdoor walking can become dangerous, even deadly. Extreme heat increases the likelihood of heat exhaustion, heat stroke, dehydration, and cardiovascular complications. Heat-related poor air quality present risks for those with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Warmer weather also leads to a larger number of mosquitoes and ticks, increasing exposure to infectious diseases such as Lyme disease. In such conditions, walking outdoors no longer promotes health but instead poses significant health risks.

There are widespread negative effects related to climate change. Adults of all ages report experiencing anxiety, grief, and uncertainty about environmental changes and the state of the planet. Eco anxiety (Kurt & Pihkala, 2022) is widespread and increases anxiety and depression in people of all ages and backgrounds (Monsour et al., 2022). Although much of the research on eco-anxiety has focused on younger populations, older adults are vulnerable, particularly when the consequence of extreme weather is increasingly evident and poses a threat not only to their own well-being but that of future generations.

The effects of climate change are no longer abstract or distant. They are experienced daily. During the early summer days of 2026, there have already been many days when heat and poor air quality have resulted in situations where older adults were advised to remain indoors, limiting opportunities for walking, exercise, and social interaction. For Dina and many others who depend on daily walks to maintain both physical health and social connection, repeated periods of extreme heat will increase sedentary behavior and lead to social isolation, and loneliness. For all of us, it is important to take steps to help combat climate change, to help increase the availability of accessible and safe walking spaces, to plant trees and shrubs when we can, and to recognize that all of our well-being depends on being able to walk outside.

"As you start to walk on the way, the way appears."

Rumi, 13th-century Persian poet

item.title: When Every Doctor Got It Wrong
item.description:
Psychiatry

When Every Doctor Got It Wrong

Personal Perspective: When psychiatric diagnosis misses the cause of symptoms.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Psychiatric diagnosis relies on symptom checklists, not on identifying underlying causes of suffering.
  • Misdiagnosis doesn't just delay treatment—the wrong medications can actively worsen the illness.
  • The people closest to the patient often ask the questions the clinical system is not designed to ask.
  • When the map is wrong, every step taken in good faith carries the patient further from help.
Source: Allen Boguslavsky / Pexels

Dr. H’s office sat high above Michigan Avenue in Chicago, and on clear days the view took in a long sweep of the city I loved—the lake flat and silver to the east, the grid of streets extending westward. The office itself was full of books and small sculptures, the room of a man who believed the psyche was a thing worth taking seriously. I had found this reassuring once.

By the summer of 2016, sitting in the chair across from his desk, I could no longer feel the city below as something that belonged to me.

When I asked him what he thought was wrong with me, he offered two diagnoses: major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. Both came from the DSM, psychiatry’s diagnostic manual. Both were delivered with the confidence of a man who had practiced for 40 years.

Neither fit.

For over three decades, I had never experienced depression for any significant stretch of time. I was constitutionally, almost aggressively optimistic—the friend people called when they needed cheering up, not the one who called in distress. Anxiety before a lecture or a deadline, yes, but a clinical disorder? The labels felt like a coat cut for someone else’s body: technically mine, functionally wrong, a daily reminder that the person being treated was not quite the person who had arrived.

What I could not yet see—what no one in that room could see—was that my suffering was real but had been misidentified at its root. I was experiencing the crash side of a bipolar illness that would not be correctly named for another four years. And something else was happening that neither checklist nor clinical interview could reach: a syphilis infection, progressing quietly through my nervous system, mimicking psychiatric illness with eerie precision.

Syphilis is called "the great imitator" for a reason. It can produce anxiety, insomnia, cognitive fog, and mood instability. It can rewrite experience from the inside, molecule by molecule.

Yet no one ordered a blood test. We were speaking serotonin.

The Roulette Wheel

What followed was a high-stakes game of pharmaceutical trial and error. When one medication failed, we tried another. When trazodone brought no relief, we moved to hydroxyzine. When that did nothing, Dr. H prescribed seroquel, a powerful antipsychotic.

Each new prescription carried the implicit promise that relief lay just one adjustment away. Each failure felt less like a data point in an uncertain science and more like evidence that something was fundamentally wrong with the process itself.

The practice has a clinical name—polypharmacy—and it is widespread enough to have raised serious questions about the quality of mental healthcare in America. The wheel keeps spinning because the system is designed to treat symptoms, not to locate causes.

But Dr. H was not the only one spinning it. Over the course of four months in 2016, I was evaluated by four different hospital systems, in addition to my longtime outpatient psychiatrist. Not one of them questioned the original diagnosis. Not one ordered a comprehensive history and physical. Not one, despite my identity as a gay man in a period of high-risk sexual behavior, ordered an STD panel. Each institution accepted the labels it inherited from the last, added its own prescriptions, and passed me along.

A cardiologist who saw a patient with recurring chest pain likely wouldn't simply prescribe anti-angina medication and move on. She would investigate the cause of the pain. Yet in psychiatry, I felt like I was handed the equivalent of a pain reliever and sent home, again and again, by institution after institution.

My mother kept asking the question that none of these institutions were structured to ask: What was the source of my anxiety? Where was it coming from? She had no more answer than I did. But she was the only one asking.

The psychologist Gary Greenberg, in The Book of Woe, describes the DSM as “an anthology of suffering,” not a map of diseases but a catalog of the ways people commonly hurt. The diagnostician’s job, he writes, is to find the disease that unites scattered symptoms and “makes them manifest in precisely the way they do.” But even in the best cases, “nature gives up its secrets grudgingly.”

The DSM offers symptom checklists. It does not, in most cases, offer causes. Where every other branch of medicine categorizes illness by both its symptoms and its underlying mechanism, psychiatry can typically offer only the former. There are no blood tests, no biopsies, and no imaging studies that can isolate depression or bipolar disorder. Those diseases cannot be found in tissue.

This made my diagnosis a particular kind of trap. The labels were not "wrong" the way a misread X-ray is wrong. They were incomplete in a more dangerous way: They described what I appeared to be suffering while actively obscuring what was causing it.

And unfortunately, the antidepressants prescribed to treat my supposed unipolar depression were the very class of drugs known to destabilize a bipolar brain. Each prescription, written in good faith, pushed me further into the illness it was supposed to be pulling me out of.

Source: Haley Lawrence/Unsplash

The Question No One Asked

Four months after I left Dr. H’s care, I nearly died. A suicidal overdose left me in a coma for six days. The drugs I swallowed one Monday morning were the very ones that had been prescribed to help me: trazodone, seroquel, lexapro, buspar. The instruments of treatment became the instruments of crisis.

When the blood test was finally drawn in the aftermath, the syphilis diagnosis arrived not as a surprise but as a kind of grim revelation. The body had been keeping score all along.

Even then, the system did not course-correct. The psychiatric team that treated me for three weeks after the overdose conducted no deeper investigation. They did not explore whether earlier manic episodes, which were present in my history, had anyone looked, might point to a different diagnosis. My mother asked to be present during their assessments. They declined. They did not interview her or my father independently. They discharged me with the same diagnostic labels and the same class of medications.

I do not tell this story to indict any single clinician. The historian Anne Harrington has written that biological psychiatry, by the early 21st century, had “overreached, overpromised, overdiagnosed, overmedicated, and compromised its principles.” Every clinician I encountered was working precisely as they had been taught. The failure was architectural, not personal.

But the cost was personal. Years of misdiagnosis fed years of polypharmacy, which fed a destabilization that the correct diagnosis, delivered earlier, might have prevented. The bipolar disorder that no one identified until 2020 had been building throughout the years of wrong prescriptions. The syphilis that no one tested for had been inflaming a brain already vulnerable to mood disorder. The two conditions fed each other in a spiral that the system’s symptom-first architecture was not designed to interrupt.

What my mother was asking—where is this coming from?—was the question that could have interrupted it. Not because she had clinical training in psychiatry, but because she knew me. She held the longitudinal knowledge of who I had been before the illness arrived: optimistic, driven, constitutionally incapable of the depression I was being told I had. That knowledge was a diagnostic instrument the system did not know how to use.

The coat Dr. H handed me was not made for my body. But it was the only coat the system had. And so I wore it, and the wearing of it carried me further from help with every passing month toward a manual that had been stitching coats like mine for decades, and whose seams, as I would come to learn, had never held.

item.title: Random Acts of Friendship
item.description:
Friends

Random Acts of Friendship

Why small, random gestures are powerful ways to maintain friendships.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Proximity builds friendship because nearness predicts connection more than compatibility.
  • Distance doesn't end a friendship, but it turns upkeep from passive to intentional.
  • Small, unscheduled gestures often matter more than planned check-ins.
  • Friendship grows through consistent small acts, not grand occasions.
Finding the time to connect
Source: Photo by Markcos Gonçalves / Pexels

One of the things I've realized as I get older is that friendships really do matter. There is something comforting about knowing that if something went wrong, there would be a group of people ready, willing, and able to help out.

Beyond the help, friendship makes life more enjoyable. Not in some magical, one-off way, but in the seemingly random ways that surprise you. A text that arrives at the right moment. A favor offered before you asked. A joke that lands so well it carries you through the rest of the day.

Even better is the spur of the moment hangouts where the world aligns and you can hang out with your friend simply by stopping by their house to drop off your new book and catch up.

Why Proximity Matters

Friendship isn't just about who you like, although that’s important, for sure. In some cases, it's about who you're near.

A 2022 study out of Florida Atlantic University tracked friendships in elementary school classrooms over several months. The researchers found that kids seated next to or near each other were more likely to become friends than kids seated across the room, and when seating charts changed, new friendships formed along the new seating lines. The finding wasn't about compatibility. It was about proximity doing the work that intention usually gets credit for.

Adults aren't that different. We just trade classroom seats for cubicles, gyms, and coffee shops. The friends I see most often aren't necessarily the ones I have the most in common with. They're the ones I keep running into. Proximity creates the repeated, low-stakes contact that (male) friendship needs to take root, and it does most of that work quietly, before either person notices it's happening.

That's the uncomfortable part for men especially. We like to think friendship is a matter of finding the right people. Often it's a matter of putting ourselves in the right rooms, repeatedly, and letting the rest happen on its own.

To be clear, those rooms do need to have men in them that we have things in common with but, as I have written about before, showing up consistently is something that is a prerequisite for male friendship formation.

When You Can't Be Close

Proximity is a great engine for friendship, but it isn't the only one, and it isn't always available. People move. Jobs change. Kids grow up and take the built-in social structure of school pickup and Little League with them. At some point, most of us end up with good friends who live nowhere near us.

This is where a lot of men quietly let friendships lapse. Without a shared location doing the work, keeping the friendship alive requires someone to do it on purpose, and "on purpose" is exactly the kind of relational labor men are rarely trained for.

Psychology Today contributor Lydia Denworth wrote about this shift during the pandemic, when in-person contact disappeared and people had to lean on calls and video chats to keep friendships alive. What she found is instructive beyond the pandemic itself: Distance doesn't have to end a friendship, but it does change what maintaining it requires. It stops being passive. It has to become a habit, the same way going to the gym is a habit, not a feeling you wait to have.

The men who keep long-distance friendships alive aren't the ones with the deepest conversations. They're the ones who've built a small, repeatable ritual: the same phone call every few weeks, the same group text, the same annual trip. The structure carries the friendship when proximity no longer can.

Random Acts of Friendship

Here's what I've noticed, though. The friendships that mean the most to me aren't sustained only by scheduled calls or standing rituals. They're kept alive by small, unscheduled gestures that show up when I least expect them.

A friend sends an article he read and thought I'd find it funny. Another texts a photo from a trip we took a decade ago, with no caption except "remember this." One shows up at my door with a bag of coffee or better yet, donuts, because he happened to be in the neighborhood.

None of these are grand gestures. None of them required planning. That's exactly what makes them work. A random act of friendship carries a message that a scheduled one can't quite send: I thought of you when I didn't have to.

This matters more for men than we tend to admit. Men are taught that reaching out needs a reason. A birthday. A crisis. A logistical need. Random acts of friendship strip away the requirement for a reason. They say, in effect, that the friendship itself is reason enough. That's a small thing to say out loud, but it's a hard thing for a lot of men to say at all, which is part of what I get into in The Male Friendship Experience.

It's the Small Things That Matter

None of this requires a grand plan. It requires attention.

Notice when something reminds you of a friend, and send it before the impulse passes. Show up somewhere he already is, instead of scheduling something new. Say the small thing instead of holding it for a better moment, because the better moment rarely comes on its own.

Friendship, in the end, isn't built primarily on the big occasions. It's built on the accumulation of small, unglamorous, often random acts that say someone is on your mind. Proximity gets you in the room. What you do once you're there, and what you do when you're not, is what keeps the friendship alive.

item.title: What Is the Story of Your Life, and What Stories Capture It?
item.description:
Identity

What Is the Story of Your Life, and What Stories Capture It?

There are myths and fairy tales about whatever themes dominate your life.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • The recurring themes in your life or personality have parallels in myths and fairy tales.
  • Myths and fairy tales are stories of transformation, and offer insights and inspiration for your own journey.
  • Myths get at the heart of human behavior, at profound truths and ageless patterns—including your own.
  • Myths aren’t falsehoods. They aren’t literally true, but psychologically true.
Source: Pixabay

If you’ve ever heard yourself say “That’s the story of my life,” there’s probably a literal story—a fairy tale, a myth, even a novel—that would capture it, helping you understand it and maybe retell it.

For example, if the story of your life is one of constantly taking the weight of the world onto your shoulders, you’re recapitulating the story of Atlas. If you’re often brought down by your pride or over-ambition, you’re living out the myth of Icarus, who flew too close to the sun and plunged to earth. If you've overcome tremendous obstacles in your life, you're living out the story of the Phoenix rising. You’re channeling Pandora when your curiosity keeps getting you into trouble, Sisyphus when your efforts feel futile and never-ending, Narcissus when you’re overly self-involved, Superman when you imagine yourself invincible, Ahab when you’re undone by your own anger, and Jonah when you’re constantly running from a calling.

The Odyssey isn’t just Ulysses’ story, nor The Wizard of Oz just Dorothy’s. They’re accounts of anyone struggling to find their way home. Bilbo Baggins is anyone who feels compelled to leave behind the familiar for a greater cause. Exodus is about any kind of deliverance from bondage.

The Relevance of Myths and Fairy Tales to Modern Life

article continues after advertisement

No matter what themes dominate your life (trying to change the world, seeking purpose or power, gaining love, finding yourself, healing a wound) and no matter what traits dominate your personality (independence, competitiveness, compassion, fear, stubbornness, enthusiasm, narcissism), you can find striking parallels to them—as well as insights, inspiration and cautionary tales—in the world of myths and fairy tales, and in the characters who people those stories.

Myths are not, as most people suppose, synonymous with falsehoods and fanciful exaggerations, as in “The Myth of the Middle Class” or “Ten Myths About Parenting,” though they are a bit like fiction in the sense that both involve stories that aren’t factual but they’re true. They aren’t literally true, but psychologically true. They didn’t really happen, but they’re happening all the time.

They’re also stories we’ve been prepared to encounter from childhood, when we were read nursery rhymes—the pre-school of fairy tales and myths. And both begin with “Once upon a time,” meaning not just a time that once was, but this time right now, and all the time yet to come.

How Classic Stories Parallel Everyday Struggles

In our modern re-enactments, the battlefields can be quite ordinary. They don’t take place in the Land of Oz or a mysterious island in the Aegean, and they don’t pit the hero or heroine against dragons or cyclops or armies of flying monkeys. Instead, they take place in your home or office, your relationships to your loved ones, your career, your rebellious teenagers, your health. And the outcomes are capable of making or breaking you as surely as did the trials of Ulysses, Luke Skywalker, Dorothy and Goldilocks.

These stories get at the heart of human behavior, at profound truths, universal themes, and ageless patterns—including your own. They’re what are called archetypal truths—eternally recurring truths. And whether they’re Norse sagas, Siberian shamanic tales, Greek epics, or Biblical fables, they’re above all stories of transformation: from sleep to awakening, folly to wisdom, woundedness to wholeness, from being lost to finding your way. And like dreams and body symptoms, they offer clues, directions and solutions. They don’t just diagnose; they prescribe.

article continues after advertisement

How to Use Mythology to Inspire Personal Change

To whatever degree you may be seeking transformation in your own life, and counsel on how to achieve it, you might consider identifying “the story of your life”—or at least the dominant themes in your life and personality—and curling up with those stories that capture it.

For instance, if you seek to awaken in some way, and not continually sleep-walk through life, you might find inspiration—and expert tutoring—for such a crusade in stories about King Arthur, Sleeping Beauty, or the Grail King, because they all speak to the archetypal idea that when the king sleeps, those around him also sleep and the kingdom goes to sleep. When the queen sleeps, those around her also sleep and the kingdom goes dormant. But when the king and queen awaken, those around them also awaken, and the kingdom begins to flower.

This idea is built very deeply into the mythologies, psychologies, philosophies and religions of the world, and the point is this: when you awaken, you help the kingdom awaken. Your individual work is the work of the world, it does begin in your own backyard, and the small steps are the big picture.

Rewrite Your Life as a Hero’s Journey

For a deeper dive, you might even consider re-telling the story of your life as a myth or fairy tale. If you choose the most persistent type of myth in the catalog—what mythologist Joseph Campbell called the “hero’s journey”—you would cast yourself as the hero or heroine, and your earthly struggles as plot twists in an epic adventure.

article continues after advertisement

The transformation you seek becomes the goal of your quest, the obstacles become the tests of your endurance and resilience, friends and mentors become your allies and guardians, and you’d get to see the Big Picture of your life, the way it appears from the pressbox on Mount Olympus where the gods sip mint juleps and watch The Game.

Before sitting down for a writing session, consider the following ingredients of the typical hero’s journey:

* Hero/heroine: Are you a king or queen, prince or princess, space traveller, monk, prisoner, farm-girl, fisherman, wild animal or house-cat?

* Ordinary World: Where you start the adventure—your familiar surroundings, situations, relationships and beliefs.

* The Call to Adventure: There’s a sudden knock on the door—or a dream, an inner voice, an illness—and you’re confronted with an adventure to undertake, defining the change you seek.

* Refusal of the Call: Phase one of responding to a call is typically running from it. You find yourself afraid of the unknown, turning down the quest, playing small, distracting yourself. Here you define your hesitation or avoidance, your fear of the quest.

* Allies: Anyone or anything that pulls you through the fear, and then continues to inspire, provoke, teach, test, train and protect you; who brings the sense of trust to your journey.

* Obstacles: Whatever thwarts or tests you on the journey, from within or without. They may be demons and dragons, witches and warlords, but don’t necessarily confuse them with enemies. They may be allies in thick disguise, the same way setbacks often lead to breakthroughs.

* Supreme Ordeal: The hero’s journey typically includes a confrontation with your greatest fear. Whether you’re inside the Death Star or the castle of the Wicked Witch, you encounter here a physical or psychological make-or-break moment.

* Return: Coming back to the Ordinary World from your journey, you share the boons of your quest with others—a new status quo, a new story, a higher order of functioning, a reconciliation, a treasure.

article continues after advertisement

* Final Exam: The Return often provokes a last test to see whether you’ve really changed or are just coasting on a kind of workshop high; a last chance for the forces of darkness to strike back at the triumphant hero, as the evil Saruman did against Frodo at the end of The Lord of the Rings.

Whichever myths or fairy tales you consult in order to better understand the story of your life, remember what the poet Stanley Kunitz once said of these stories: "Old myths, old gods, old heroes have never died. They are only sleeping at the bottom of our mind, waiting for our call."

item.title: Why Social Media Affects Body Image Differently
item.description:
Body Image

Why Social Media Affects Body Image Differently

How appearance concerns reflect broader life priorities.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Social media’s impact on body image varies by life orientation and gender.
  • People with a slower life history strategy report more positive body image.
  • Heavier social media use is connected to a higher appearance focus but lower appearance satisfaction.

It is now almost common sense to say that social media affects how people feel about their appearance. We scroll through edited faces, idealized bodies, cosmetic transformations, fitness routines, and carefully staged lifestyles. It is difficult not to compare.

But comparison is only part of the story. In our recent study of nearly 9,000 Arab-speaking young adults, we found that body image is also related to something deeper: people’s broader orientation toward life, the future, relationships, and self-investment. In psychology, this is often discussed through life history theory.

Life history theory sounds technical, but the basic idea is straightforward. All of us have limited time, energy, and attention. We cannot invest equally in everything. Some people, often shaped by more unpredictable or competitive environments, become more oriented toward immediate rewards, social competition, and short-term opportunities. This is called a faster life history strategy. Others are more oriented toward long-term planning, stability, self-control, health, education, and future investment. This is called a slower life history strategy. The Mini-K scale used in our study captures these tendencies, with higher scores indicating a slower strategy. This framework helps us think differently about appearance.

Appearance is not trivial. It is one of the most visible parts of social life. People use grooming, clothing, cosmetics, fitness, posture, and other forms of appearance enhancement to communicate attractiveness, identity, confidence, status, and belonging. The key question is not simply whether people care about appearance, but why they care.

Our findings suggest that people with slower life history strategies reported more positive evaluations of their appearance. They were more satisfied with how they looked. They also reported greater appearance orientation, meaning that they paid attention to grooming and self-presentation. This is important because it shows that caring about appearance is not necessarily the same as being dissatisfied with appearance. Appearance investment can reflect self-care and confidence, not only insecurity.

By contrast, more time spent on social media was associated with lower appearance satisfaction but greater appearance orientation. In simpler terms, heavier social media use was linked to thinking more about appearance while feeling less satisfied with it. Social media may therefore make appearance more central, more public, and more competitive. It does not simply expose people to beauty ideals; it creates an environment where appearance is constantly displayed, evaluated, and compared.

This is where life history theory becomes especially useful. A faster life orientation may make people more sensitive to immediate social rewards, attractiveness, and competition. In an appearance-saturated digital environment, that sensitivity may translate into more comparison and lower body satisfaction. A slower life orientation, by contrast, may be linked to more future-oriented self-care and less dependence on immediate social feedback. In our analyses, screen time partly explained the pathway between life history strategy and body image, especially among women. Slower-oriented women spent less time on social media, which was associated with more positive body image and less appearance preoccupation.

Figure 1. Association between life-history strategy and appearance evaluation by nationality.
Source: Farid Pazhoohi

Figure 1 (not included in our original paper) helps make this point visually. It shows that the positive relationship between slower life history strategy and appearance satisfaction appears across different countries in the sample. This matters because it suggests that the finding is not simply driven by one national group. The paper’s mixed-effect models also showed that country-level variation was small, indicating that appearance evaluation and appearance orientation were broadly similar across nationalities.

The sex difference is also important. Figure 2 shows that the relationship between life history strategy and appearance evaluation was positive for both men and women, but stronger among women. In other words, slower life history strategy was linked to greater appearance satisfaction in both sexes, but this association was especially pronounced among women. Females also reported higher appearance orientation, suggesting greater investment in appearance management.

Figure 2. The relationship between life-history strategy and appearance evaluation for males and females.
Source: Farid Pazhoohi

This does not mean that women are simply “more appearance-focused” in a superficial sense. Rather, it reflects the broader social reality that women often face stronger appearance pressures. For women, appearance can become a more consequential domain of social evaluation, comparison, and self-presentation. The finding that slower-oriented women showed particularly positive appearance evaluations suggests that future-oriented self-care may be psychologically different from competitive appearance monitoring.

Body image is not only a media problem or an individual self-esteem problem. It is part of a larger system involving social comparison, gendered expectations, cultural values, evolved motives, and digital environments. Social media matters, but it does not affect everyone in the same way. Its effects may depend partly on how people are already oriented toward competition, self-presentation, and the future. In the end, the question is not whether appearance matters. It clearly does. The better question is: What kind of relationship do we have with our appearance? This question also connects with some themes in my forthcoming book on appearance enhancement: why humans care about how they look, and how appearance becomes part of social perception and everyday interaction.
